newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Christopher says quick, significant action needed.
newsitem.headline: Christopher says quick, significant action needed.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher said he will tell Israeli and Palestinian leaders on Sunday it is urgent that they quickly produce significant results in resumed peace talks.
Christopher was on his way to Israel on Saturday for a hastily-arranged 27-hour stopover.

He is due to see Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat before they resume Middle East peace talks on Sunday at the Erez border crossing between Israel and Gaza.
Christopher said that following this week's emergency summit in Washington he felt he could not embark on a planned nine-day Africa trip without again meeting Netanyahu and Arafat.
The two-day crisis summit produced no results beyond agreement to reopen negotiations on the 1993 Oslo peace accord that gave Palestinians self-rule in Gaza and the West Bank.
Christopher and other senior officials maintain this is an important step if violence, which has cooled in recent days, is to be kept in check and the peace process is to move forward.

"From a personal standpoint I felt I did not want to launch on the Africa trip ... without another opportunity to meet with the parties and stress those three points," he told reporters on his aircraft from Washington.
Those points are "the importance of significant progress, the urgency of it and especially a reminder of their commitment that they would become personally involved if progress wasn't made", he said.
U.S. officials would not be precise on how quickly progress must be made but one said it would take more than a couple of days.

Christopher, whose plane refuelled at Shannon Airport, was due in Israel on Sunday morning. He said he would meet Netanyahu in Jerusalem at 3 p.m. (1200 GMT) and then travel to Erez to meet Arafat at 6 p.m. (1500 GMT)
Although he will be in Erez, officials said Christopher would not attend the opening of the peace talks themselves.
Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring is heading for Israel and Gaza on Sunday on a mission ordered by European Union leaders frustrated at being cut out of U.S.-brokered peace efforts.
Arafat appealed this week for EU involvement in efforts to rebuild the peace process.
Irish officials said Spring would convey the EU's desire to see the Israelis and Palestinians to make further efforts to patch up the peace process.

But U.S. officials said they did not expect Spring to be in Erez. U.S. Mideast Coordinator Dennis Ross, negotiator of Arab-Israeli peace issues for more than seven years, will "facilitate" the negotiations.

Asked about a possible European role, Christopher said: "It's clear the Europeans have a very strong and legitimate interest in these negotiations. In a major way it's exactly the same interest as ours."
He noted Europeans are major financial backers of Palestinians and said Europe's call for Netanyahu and Arafat to resolve differences over their peace deal was positive.
But Christopher seemed cool to a direct European role, saying "any major change in the bilateral character of these negotiations is not likely to take place".
He defended U.S. plans to maintain a continual presence as facilitator at the negotiations, saying Washington has a history of assisting the parties and knows the agreements very well.
U.S. officials worry that bringing in more participants will only make the process more complicated and unwieldy.
Christopher said the Erez talks will focus on implementing the Israeli-Palestinian "interim agreement" reached at Oslo and not with final-status issues like Jerusalem.
Israel's decision to open a tunnel near Moslem and Jewish holy sites in Jerusalem sparked clashes two weeks ago with Palestinians angered over the slow pace of peace.
Hebron tops the agenda. Israel was to withdraw its troops from the West Bank town last March but has not done so.
Officials said Ross will help the two sides shape the agenda and shuttle between the two sides, helping them understand eath other's proposals.
